title: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
content:
The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Big Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game.
This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the issue in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance “declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity.”
Noting “a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools,” the group of jurors called out AI’s ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still “not a foregone conclusion in our industry.”
The jurors also urged the IGF as a whole to “adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work.”
The big walkback
Although the jurors’ statement didn’t name any specific games, by Tuesday morning, one critical darling in particular was increasingly being noted as a central part of the debate. In a statement provided to Aftermath (and added to the game’s FAQ page shortly thereafter), developer House House admitted publicly that “LLMs were used sparingly” near the end of Big Walk‘s development “to help work through some difficult technical challenges and bugs.”
That limited AI use—which House House says represents “well under 0.1% of Big Walk‘s code—stemmed in part from a thorny Unity engine bug that was slowing the game down with “infinite length” shadows during some game situations. After consulting with a Unity engineer who determined a fix “wasn’t possible,” House House said it consulted an LLM chatbot, which suggested a possible fix that the developers “had to modify… extensively” into the 10 lines of code that ended up in the final game (At least one social media user says the bug was indeed fixable with significant human effort, though).

report.summary: House House's belated disclosure of minimal LLM use in Big Walk has ignited an indie game industry fight over AI disclosure, labor, and awards eligibility.
report.background: AI tools have spread quickly through game development, from art and writing to debugging, but disclosure norms remain unsettled. Indie developers often face tight budgets and deadlines, making AI assistants attractive even for small technical tasks. The Independent Games Festival is a prestigious showcase for indie work, and its jury process has become a flashpoint. For months, judges discussed growing generative-AI submissions behind the scenes. The debate went public when jurors split over whether any AI use should disqualify a game. The controversy reflects broader tensions over labor, ecology, artistic authorship, and trust between developers and players.
key_points: Nineteen members of the Independent Games Festival jury signed a statement declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity. They cited ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms, and urged the IGF to adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future awards.

Big Walk developer House House admitted that LLMs were used sparingly near the end of development, representing well under 0.1% of the game's code. The AI helped address a Unity engine bug that caused infinite-length shadows, after a Unity engineer reportedly said a fix was not possible.

House House said the LLM's suggested fix had to be modified extensively into about 10 lines of final code. At least one social media user argued the bug was fixable with significant human effort, raising questions about the necessity and framing of the disclosure.

The disclosure came only after public pressure, highlighting the lack of clear industry norms around AI use and responsible disclosure. Even minimal AI assistance can now affect awards eligibility, reputation, and trust in the indie game community.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the dispute shows that transparency and provenance will matter as much as capability. Tool makers may face pressure to help developers document AI-assisted work. For developers, even tiny LLM use can become a reputational and awards risk, so studios need clear internal policies, records, and disclosure language. For regular users, the fight signals that AI disclosure is becoming part of consumer trust, especially in creative fields where labor and authorship concerns run deep. Awards bodies may become de facto regulators of AI use, shaping what tools developers admit to using.
report.tools: To follow up, watch the IGF's submission rules and AI disclosure policies, Unity's issue tracker and forums for engine bugs, and AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code. Open-source options like Continue.dev and Aider offer more auditable local workflows. Game-credit and disclosure databases can also help track how studios describe AI assistance.
